body_html:
Update:

  • Aug4’26: Q2 2026 Earnings Results & Revised target ($60 → $62)

TLDR

  • CSTM is a downstream aluminium converter: it rolls and extrudes metal into engineered products for aerospace, beverage cans and cars, passing the aluminium price through to customers and keeping a conversion margin.

  • The bull case: a decade of repair has produced record earnings power. FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA of $720M ex metal lag was followed by a Q1 2026 all-time record of $262M and a raised 2026 guide of $900M to $940M, while the balance sheet sits at 2.2x levered with no maturities until 2028 and a $300M buyback running to 2028.

  • The key risk: a chunk of the 2026 windfall is temporary. Scrap spreads, tariff-inflated US metal premiums and a competitor’s plant fire all helped, and 2027 could show an air pocket when they fade.

  • Verdict: BUY. The model values CSTM at $60, a near double, with a $20 bear case for an R/R of 1 to 2.9. Pricing management’s own windfall-free 2028 targets still gets me $50.

  • RankedStocks scores CSTM an Elite 83, with near-perfect Sentiment (96) and Outlook (98) against depressed trailing Growth (32) and Profitability (34): the same trailing-versus-forward mismatch the whole thesis rests on.

Table of Contents

  • How does this stock rank?

  • From near-death to record year

  • How the business actually makes money

  • The record quarter, decomposed

  • The crown jewel

  • The problem child grows up

How does this stock rank?

Constellium [] scores 83 on RankedStocks, an Elite rating (the top band starts at 80), and sits in the 89th percentile of both its country group and the materials sector.

The factor split underneath is what makes the score worth reading, because it maps onto the argument of this deep dive with unusual precision.

Valuation 51. Neutral, and fair: after a double off the November lows the stock no longer screens as statistically cheap against materials peers on trailing multiples. The gap the model finds sits in what the trailing multiple can’t see, the durable earnings base, the deleveraging and the buyback, so a middling Valuation score is what a half-finished re-rating looks like.

Growth 32. This is the trailing five years talking: revenue fell 8.3% in 2023 and 6.3% in 2024 before the 15.2% recovery in 2025, so the CAGR math is still dragging the trough around. The forward build (+4% to +5% revenue growth on the aerospace ramp and packaging trend) hasn’t entered the trailing window yet.

Profitability 34. Same mechanism. Trailing margins still carry 2024’s 7.8% EBITDA margin and years of thin net income, and adjusted ROIC only crossed 9% in 2025. If the durable EBITDA base holds near $900M, this score improves mechanically as the trough quarters roll out of the data.

Sentiment 96 and Outlook 98. The forward-looking half of the framework is close to perfect, reflecting the guidance raise, the record Q1 and the estimate revisions that follow both.

That shape (weak trailing factors, near-perfect forward factors, Elite composite) is the quantitative version of this article’s thesis: the backward-looking scores describe the company the market remembers, and the forward-looking ones describe the company management is running.

You can run this framework on any ticker yourself, for free, at RankedStocks.com.

From near-death to record year

Constellium was carved out of Rio Tinto’s downstream aluminium operations in January 2011, when Apollo took 51% and France’s strategic investment fund took 10% (Rio Tinto kept 39% and sold the residual stake down around the 2013 IPO). It listed on the NYSE in May 2013 at $15 a share. Then it nearly destroyed itself. In January 2015 it paid $1.4B, including $945M of assumed debt, for Wise Metals, the owner of the Muscle Shoals rolling mill in Alabama. Within a year it had written off €400M of the deal (the Wise impairment disclosed in the FY2015 results and the FY2015 20-F). By the end of 2016, book equity was negative €570M…

… net leverage was above 5x…

...and the shares traded in the low single digits.

Jean-Marc Germain took over as CEO in July 2016 and spent a decade repairing the damage: fixing Muscle Shoals operationally, buying out the UACJ stake in the Bowling Green body-sheet plant in 2019, converting to a French SE domiciled in Paris, and grinding leverage down from above 5x into the company’s 1.5x to 2.5x target range. Equity went from negative €570M to positive €826M at the end of 2025.

The stock, thirteen years after the IPO, has doubled its offer price.

That’s the whole distress-to-normal arc, and I’d argue the market’s memory of the first half still prices the second.

The handover matters too. Ingrid Joerg became CEO in January 2026 after ten years inside the company. She ran the aerospace segment from 2015, when it earned less than $500 of EBITDA per tonne, then became COO in 2023. That segment earned $1,697 per tonne in Q1 2026.

How the business actually makes money

Constellium doesn’t smelt aluminium and doesn’t want to. It buys metal, casts it into slabs and billets, then rolls and extrudes it into products customers can’t easily source elsewhere: aerospace plate, canstock, automotive body sheet, crash management systems. Pricing is LME plus a regional premium plus a conversion margin. The metal component passes through to the customer, either through back-to-back purchases or hedges that hand the residual exposure to banks. What Constellium keeps is the conversion margin. Volume times conversion margin is the whole profit engine; the aluminium price itself is mostly noise.

Mostly.

Three second-order effects matter for this thesis, and they’re worth two minutes to understand because they explain both the record earnings and the bear case.

First, the metal price lag. Pass-through isn’t instant, so when aluminum prices move, reported earnings pick up a non-cash timing effect. It was +$126M in FY2025 and +$97M in Q1 2026 alone, and it cuts the other way when metal falls (it was -$92M in 2023). Management strips it from Segment Adjusted EBITDA, and so does my model. Every EBITDA number in this article excludes it unless I say otherwise.

Second, scrap spreads. Constellium is one of the largest can recyclers in the world, and it buys used beverage cans and other scrap at a discount to LME while selling at LME-based prices. When that discount widens, recycling margin expands. The 50% US aluminium tariffs pushed the Midwest premium to a record of 90 cents per pound, and since scrap is excluded from Section 232 tariffs, US scrap spreads went from historically tight in 2024 to unusually wide in 2025 and 2026. The Midwest premium averaged $1,298/t in 2025 versus $432/t in 2024, tripling y/y.

Third, the customer structure. The top ten customers are 56% of revenue, and in 2025, for the first time, two customers each crossed 10% of group sales ($943M and $852M). The names, per the prior 10-K, include Airbus, Boeing [], Ball [], Crown [], BMW, Ford [] and Mercedes. Concentration like that is a risk, and it’s also the moat: aerospace plate and body sheet require multi-year qualification, NADCAP certification and dedicated tooling. Once you’re on the platform, as management put it on the Q4 call, “it really doesn’t happen that you get substituted.”

The segments, using FY2025 numbers: A&T (Aerospace & Transportation) did $1,968M of revenue and $339M of EBITDA at a 17.2% margin, rolling plate and sheet at Issoire, Ravenswood and Sierre. P&ARP (Packaging & Automotive Rolled Products) did $5,078M of revenue and $353M of EBITDA at 7.0%, making canstock and body sheet at Muscle Shoals, Neuf-Brisach, Singen and Bowling Green. AS&I (Automotive Structures & Industry) did $1,579M of revenue and $72M of EBITDA at 4.6%, extruding crash systems and battery enclosures across fifteen smaller plants. Holdings and corporate cost $44M.

The record quarter, decomposed

Q1 2026 was the best quarter in Constellium’s history.

Revenue rose 24% y/y. EBITDA ex lag up 78% y/y and an all-time record. P&ARP printed $151M, an all-time record for any quarter and up 152% y/y. A&T printed $102M, a Q1 record. Normalized EPS of $1.20 beat consensus by $0.60.

Ten weeks after guiding 2026 EBITDA to $780M to $820M, management raised the range to $900M to $940M and lifted FCF guidance from above $200M to above $275M. Two raises inside a quarter is the sort of thing that happens when a business inflects faster than its own management expects. The trailing twelve months tell the same story: LTM segment EBITDA went from $561M at March 2025 to $835M at March 2026.

A meaningful slice of this is windfall. The P&ARP bridge shows it plainly. Of the segment’s $91M y/y improvement, $65M came through the costs line, which is where favourable metal costs, wide scrap spreads and the Midwest premium show up. Volume was actually negative.

Three tailwinds are doing the heavy lifting, and none of them is permanent.

Wide scrap spreads: the CFO has been explicit that “recycling economics have averaged out over time” and frames the swing at $15M to $20M a quarter in either direction in abnormal years; 2024 was the headwind year, 2026 is the tailwind year.

The body-sheet shortage: a fire at a competitor’s US rolling plant (Novelis’ Oswego mill) left North America short of automotive sheet, and Constellium is supplying the gap from Europe while “maxing out capacity in the US”; management expects the benefit to last through 2026, and by implication not much longer.

The tariff premium: a 50% Section 232 tariff structure inflates US metal prices, and while management believes tariffs are “going to stick,” that’s a policy assumption, and policy can reverse.

Management knows this, which is why the 2028 targets of $900M EBITDA and $300M FCF explicitly exclude today’s scrap environment and the shortage benefit. Joerg was direct on the Q4 call: “We don’t know if the current situation that we experienced in 2026 are going to last and for how long... which is why we have preferred to remain at a more prudent stance.” She has also called 2027 “a transition year,” which I read as a warning that the windfall fades before the structural projects fully land.

Strip the windfall and what’s left? My answer: a durable earnings base around management’s $900M with three structural drivers still ramping. Muscle Shoals, after a decade as the group’s problem asset, has been setting operational records since late 2024. Aerospace destocking is ending just as build rates rise. And the Vision 2028 cost programme plus $100M a year of return-seeking capex (a third casthouse for Airware alloys at Issoire, a new casting pit at Muscle Shoals, the Ravenswood casthouse modernization, the Neuf-Brisach recycling centre) adds earnings that depend on execution, on projects inside the fence, and on nobody’s tariff policy.

The crown jewel

A&T is where Constellium stops being a metals processor and becomes something closer to an aerospace supplier with a metals cost base. Issoire is one of the world’s two leading integrated aerospace plate mills by volume. Ravenswood is one of the few facilities anywhere that can roll plates large enough for the biggest commercial aircraft. The Airware aluminium-lithium alloy family is patented, and the qualification cycle for aerospace plate runs years, which is why the competitor list (Arconic, Kaiser [], Novelis) has stayed short for decades.

The margin history shows what that position is worth. Segment EBITDA per tonne has gone from under $500 in 2015 to $1,634 in FY2025 to $1,697 in Q1 2026. Management raised its through-cycle target for the segment twice in twelve months, from $1,000 to $1,100 to $1,300 per tonne.

What makes the setup attractive now is that the recent margin gains happened without aerospace volume. Aerospace rolled revenue was flat in 2025 at $1,068M because the supply chain spent two years destocking aluminium plate; A&T’s FY2025 aerospace shipments actually fell. That destocking now “appears to be easing” (management’s words, and Q1 aerospace shipments were up 13% y/y), while the demand side is as visible as aerospace demand ever gets: Airbus plans 870 deliveries in 2026 and is taking narrowbody rates to 75 a month by 2027, with Boeing moving the 737 line to 47 a month, against a combined backlog of twelve years of production. Add defence onshoring (TID shipments were up 18% in Q1) and the new Airbus multi-year extrusions contract including Airware, and the volume kicker that was missing from the 2025 margin story arrives in 2026 through 2028.

The model reflects this as A&T shipments growing 6% in 2026 and 2027, tapering to 2.5% by the mid-2030s, with segment margin rising from 17.2% to a 20% cap by 2029. For reference, the segment already earned 18.8% in 2023 during the last favourable mix period, so the cap sits 120bps above a level the segment has actually printed, on more volume and a richer plate mix.

The problem child grows up

P&ARP is the segment the market has spent a decade learning to distrust, because Muscle Shoals was the asset that nearly killed the company. That history is exactly why the current inflection is underpriced. The plant runs the widest hot line in North America and one of the world’s largest can recycling operations, and after the post-COVID years of manning and maintenance problems and a weather hit in early 2024, it has been setting operational records since late 2024. This is also where most of the group’s capex has gone: $175M of the segment’s spend in 2025, plus the new casting pit now ramping.

Demand is the stable kind. Canstock grows 2.8% a year in North America and 3.4% in Europe through 2030 per CRU, can makers are adding capacity, and aluminium keeps taking share from other substrates. On top of that base, the segment carries the body-sheet windfall discussed above, plus a structural body-sheet position through Bowling Green and Muscle Shoals that existed before the competitor fire and will exist after it.

The margin question is whether 7.0% (FY2025) can hold near the 10.2% the segment printed in Q1 2026. The model says no, deliberately: it fades the windfall and lands P&ARP at a 9.5% cap by the early 2030s. The segment did 10.6% in 2020, so the cap is again below a demonstrated peak. What carries margin higher structurally, rather than through spreads, is Muscle Shoals utilization, the recycling build-out at Neuf-Brisach (recycled input is also the trigger on the sustainability-linked notes), and mix shifting toward body sheet.

The broken corner

Segment EBITDA has nearly halved from $129M in 2023 to $72M in 2025. European auto production is weak, the Swiss Valais plants have taken impairments three years running plus a flood, and the segment’s Q1 EBITDA of $24M, while up 50% y/y, annualizes to less than $100M against $1.6B of revenue.

I treat AS&I as a cheap option rather than a pillar. The content story is real (the model assumes auto build rates grow only 1.5% a year, with aluminium content per vehicle rising faster as OEMs lightweight and battery-electric platforms carry far more extruded content than combustion cars), the crash management franchise is a global leader, and the restructuring plus Vision 2028 work gives cost recovery even without a European volume recovery. The model caps the segment at an 8% margin by 2030, at the bottom of its own 8% to 10% pre-2022 history. If Europe never recovers, the segment stays a rounding error and the thesis survives; if it normalizes, there’s +$100M of EBITDA nobody is paying for.

Management and capital allocation

The capital allocation story has three legs, and all three point the same way: per-share value.

First, buybacks over dividends. Constellium pays no dividend and has said it has no intention of starting one. Instead, it has repurchased 14.7M shares for $221M since early 2024, an average price near $15 against today’s $29, retiring 10% of the share count.

The board approved a new $300M programme in March 2026 running to December 2028, 7% of the current market cap. Shares outstanding are down from 146.8M at the end of 2023 to 135.4M.

Second, the balance sheet is no longer the story, which for this company is a milestone in itself. Net debt of $1,829M puts leverage at 2.2x, inside the 1.5x to 2.5x target and down from 3.5x only three quarters ago. There are no bond maturities until $325M comes due in 2028, the 2029 wall of $895M carries coupons of 3.125% to 3.75%, and liquidity is $904M. The model has leverage near 1x by 2028 and a net cash position by 2031, which is what funds the buyback and the debt paydown at the same time.

Third, the internal projects. Vision 2028 is the group-wide cost and productivity programme behind the 2028 targets, and the return-seeking capex slate (Issoire casthouse, Muscle Shoals casting pit, Ravenswood modernization, Neuf-Brisach recycling) is $100M a year inside a total envelope of $330M, or 3.7% of revenue, tapering to 3.3% in the model. Capex runs at 0.9x depreciation through the forecast, which is sustainable for a business whose growth is margin and mix rather than greenfield capacity.

Two housekeeping items belong here. ROIC was 11.9% in 2025, and it averaged 10.7% over the last 10 years against an 8.4% WACC, so the reinvestment creates value rather than just size.

And Constellium became a full US domestic filer on January 1, 2026 after losing foreign-private-issuer status, which puts it on 10Ks, 10Qs and US proxy rules. The index-flow speculation around that is a bonus I don’t underwrite.

Share Beating The Tide: Stock Picks That Outperform

Valuation: what the model says

The model values Constellium at $60 per share, you can view the model here, that’s a double.

Revenue grows 4.0% in 2026 to $8.8B, then tapers from 4.9% to 2.8% by the mid-2030s. That’s built bottom-up from segment shipments and price: aerospace shipments +6% near term on the build-rate ramp, packaging +3.5% against a 2.8% to 3.4% market, auto recovering to +5% mid-cycle then fading. Metal prices are held flat off the elevated 2025 base rather than extrapolated up. Nothing in the top line requires a boom; it requires aerospace deliveries that Airbus and Boeing have already sold and can demand growing at trend.

Group EBITDA margin (segment basis, ex lag) goes from 8.5% in 2025 to 10.5% in 2026 (that’s the $920M guide midpoint, taken as given) and then grinds to 11.6% terminal. The segment caps behind it are the honest part: A&T at 20% versus 18.8% printed in 2023, P&ARP at 9.5% versus 10.6% printed in 2020, AS&I at 8% versus an 8% to 10% pre-2022 history. Every cap sits at or below a level the segment has already demonstrated.

On 2028, the model’s $1,062M is deliberately above management’s $900M target because the target excludes the scrap and shortage windfalls; the model fades them through the margin caps rather than cliff-dropping them to zero in one year. That is a lean-bull choice, and I flag it as the model’s most aggressive call.

The discounting: an 8.4% WACC built from a 1.01 unlevered beta for metals and mining businesses, a 50% optimal debt-to-capital structure, a 4.5% long-term debt rate, a 4.40% risk-free rate and a 4.23% market risk premium. Cost of equity standalone is 13.3% on the levered beta of 2.1. Terminal NOPAT growth is 2.5%. The terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA of 9.3x on 2036 EBITDA. Sum it up: $4.1B of discounted forecast FCF plus $6.0B of discounted terminal value gives a $10.1B enterprise value; subtract $2.1B of debt and $19M of minorities, add $120M of cash, and equity is $8.1B over 136M shares, or $59.60, which I round to $60.

Sensitivity, since a target this far above spot deserves stress. Move the WACC 50bps in either direction and my replication of the model moves the target to $54 and $67. Cut terminal growth from 2.5% to 2.0% and it’s $56. The target isn’t a knife-edge artifact of one input; the gap to the market is too wide for that.

I rebuilt the forecast using management’s own windfall-excluded path: EBITDA flat at $900M in 2027 and 2028, no benefit from today’s scrap spreads or the shortage, then 2.5% growth forever, same WACC, same terminal math. That deliberately conservative case is worth $50 per share. The market price of $30.11 sits below it. Said differently, at today’s price you underwrite less than management’s own prudent scenario, and the record year, the aerospace ramp and the margin build all come free. The model’s implied-expectations check makes the same point from the other side: to justify $30 you need an 11% discount rate on the model’s cash flows, versus the 8.4% the business quality supports.

The stock has averaged 5.9x EV/EBITDA over the past five years, a multiple that embeds the distress decade forever. My $60 requires that multiple to re-rate toward 9x as leverage heads below 1x, FCF compounds at a near 7% yield on the guided $275M, and the buyback removes float. Multiples follow balance sheets in this sector; the discount existed for a reason and the reason is being retired.

Catalysts: what closes the gap

A $60 target on a $30 stock only matters if something forces the market to re-underwrite the business. Four catalysts do that work, and none of them requires a boom.

First, 2027 refusing to be an air pocket. This is the whole ballgame. The bear case is that stripped of the windfall, 2027 EBITDA falls back toward $800M and the stock gets sold as a cyclical rolling over. If instead 2027 prints near management’s $900M base — because Muscle Shoals, the aerospace ramp and Vision 2028 backfill what the scrap spread gives up — the “record year was a peak” thesis breaks in public, and the multiple re-rates. Every quarter that holds the base is a data point the model needs and the bear doesn’t have.

Second, the aerospace volume actually arriving. The 2025 margin story happened with aerospace shipments falling. As destocking ends and Airbus and Boeing push narrowbody rates higher into 2027, A&T gets the volume kicker on top of a $1,697-per-tonne margin, and the new Airbus extrusions and Airware contract convert to reported revenue. Aerospace is the segment the market is most willing to pay a premium multiple for; volume growth there is what pulls the group rating up.

Third, deleveraging plus the buyback compounding per-share value. The model has leverage through 1x by 2028 and net cash by 2031. In this sector multiples follow balance sheets, so each turn of deleveraging is itself a re-rating trigger, while the $300M buyback (7% of the market cap) retires float into rising FCF. A near-7% FCF yield on the guided $275M, spent on a shrinking share count, lifts per-share value even before any multiple change.

Fourth, the US-filer transition. Constellium became a full US domestic filer on January 1, 2026, moving onto 10Ks, 10Qs and US proxy rules. Cleaner, more frequent US disclosure widens the potential US institutional owner base and opens index-inclusion optionality that a foreign private issuer did not have. I don’t underwrite the index flow, but it is a free call option on the re-rating.

Steel-manning the bear

First, the windfall. Scrap spreads mean-revert (the CFO says so himself), Oswego’s capacity comes back in 2027, and a tariff softening would compress the Midwest premium that tripled in 2025. Stack those and 2027 EBITDA could fall below 2026 rather than grow the 6.6% the model assumes. Joerg calling 2027 “a transition year” is management preparing the ground. If 2027 prints $800M against a market expecting momentum, the stock’s first reaction won’t wait for 2028.

Second, aerospace timing risk. The volume recovery leans on Airbus and Boeing actually hitting build rates they have missed for most of a decade, and on destocking ending rather than pausing. Management itself pushed the destocking recovery “to the right” during 2025. If the ramp slips a year, A&T’s margin holds but the growth kicker in the model’s 6% shipment assumption doesn’t show up.

Third, Europe stays broken. Half the footprint is European. EU auto production may never return to trend, Chinese OEMs building in Hungary and Turkey use more steel-intensive designs, and energy costs plus CBAM (which Joerg has publicly called flawed) keep European conversion structurally disadvantaged. In that world AS&I never reaches 8%, the Valais impairments keep coming, and P&ARP’s European half grinds sideways.

Fourth, the balance sheet is better, and still not clean. Gross debt is $2.0B, there’s a $362M net pension and OPEB liability, $430M of factored receivables sit off the balance sheet (unwinding them would consume real working capital, which is exactly what the model’s 2027 receivables normalization shows), and the French domicile carries tax friction: the 2025 effective rate hit 32.6% on the French surtax, and a new French tax examination opened in February 2026.

Fifth, concentration. Two customers are each above 10% of revenue and the top ten are 56%. Can-maker consolidation and OEM purchasing power both press on conversion margins over time, and a dedicated asset like Bowling Green has exactly one natural customer set.

And the overhang that doesn’t get a number: this stock has already doubled in eight months.

The marginal buyer at $30 is being asked to believe a record year is a base, in a sector where record years have historically been sold. On the model’s own trough math (a 7% to 8% conversion margin and a 4x multiple), fair value in a 2027 downturn scenario is about $20. That’s the bear case I size against, and it’s a real one: 33% down against 98% up is asymmetric, and it is still a one-in-three drawdown if the cycle rolls before the re-rating lands.

Verdict

BUY, target $60, bear case $20, R/R 1 to 2.9 from the last close of $30.11. The market is still pricing the company that bought Wise Metals, and management is running the company that fixed it. When a stock trades below the value of its own management’s most conservative plan, you’re being paid to wait for everyone else’s memory to fade.

If this walk changed how you look at converters, share it with a friend who still thinks this is an aluminum bet.
